## Overview

The National UFO Reporting Center has collected tens of thousands of reports from people who saw something in the sky they couldn't explain. Each report says when it happened, where, what the object looked like, and how long it lasted.

You're going to answer two questions:

1.  **When do people see UFOs?** Time of day, day of the week, time of year.
2.  **How long does a sighting last?**

A few things:

1.  Add `#| echo: false` to your code blocks.
2.  Use a new block when you move to a new task.
3.  Code goes in the blocks. **Answers go outside them**, as prose. A comment inside a code chunk is not an answer.
4.  Keep the original columns. Every cleaned or parsed version goes in a **new** column.

Due Monday at 8pm.

# Part 1: When do people see UFOs?

## Read the dates

Look at the first several values of `date_time`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

head(ufo$date_time, 10)
```

> What format does it appear to use?
>
> it looks like it's formatted to be month/day/year by hour to minute

"01/12/1999 22:00" could be January 12th or December 1st. You can't tell from that value alone.

> Find evidence in the data itself that settles which reading is right. What would a value need to look like to rule one reading out? Write the code that finds those values.
>
> this code proves that the first a number is the day not month

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

ufo %>%
  mutate(
    month_day = mdy_hm(data_time, quiet = TRUE),
    day_month = dmy_hm(data_time, quiet = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    month_day_missing = sum(is.na(month_day)),
    day_month_missing = sum(is.na(day_month))
  )
```

## Parse them

Create a new column, `observed_at`, containing the parsed date and time. Keep `date_time`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo:false

ufo <- ufo %>%
  mutate(
    observed_at = mdy_hm(date_time, quiet = TRUE)
  )
```

These times are local to wherever the sighting happened, e.g., Phoenix, Boston, and Anchorage, and the data doesn't record which time zone. You only need the hour, the day, and the date for this assignment, so parse **without** setting a time zone. R will label the result UTC. That isn't true either. It's just a consistent label.

> Why would setting `tz = "America/New_York"` for every sighting be a false claim?
>
> it would take away from different areas and time zones

> Since you're only using hour of day and calendar date, does the label change any of your answers? When would it?
>
> no because I'm not working at converting the time zones and sightings. it could if we wanted to see if any sightings happened at the same time across places.

## So when do people see UFOs?

Make a plot showing the number of sightings by hour of day.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

hour_plot <- ufo %>%
  filter(!is.na(observed_at)) %>%
  mutate(hour = hour(observed_at)) %>%
  count(hour)

ggplot(hour_plot, aes(x = hour, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "UFO Sightings by Hour of the Day",
    x = "Hour of the Day",
    y = "# of Sightings"
  )
```

> When do people see UFOs? Is that what you'd expect? Why might it look like this?

> most people see them later at night, which is what I would guess it would be. seeing something that is different and bright would be easier at nightime than in the day.

# Part 2: How long does a sighting last?

## Look at how durations were written

Count the distinct values of `described_encounter_length` and look at the most common ones.

top 3; 5 min, 2 min, 10 min

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false 

ufo %>%
  distinct(described_encounter_length) %>%
  arrange(described_encounter_length) %>%
  head(35)

ufo %>%
  count(described_encounter_length, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(25)
```

Create a new column, `duration_clean`, that standardizes case and whitespace. Keep the original.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

ufo <- ufo %>%
  mutate(
    duration_clean = described_encounter_length %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_squish()
  )
```

> Find three different ways an exact duration is written in `duration_clean`.
>
> 5 min, mins, minutes

> Find three descriptions that can't be turned into a single number, and say why.
>
> a few seconds, a range of time, about \# of minutes

## Recover exact minutes

Write a regular expression that identifies descriptions reporting an exact number of minutes.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
minute_pattern <- "^\\s*(\\d+(\\.\\d+)?)\\s*(minutes?|mins?)\\.?\\s*$"
```

"Exact" means a number, a minutes word, and **nothing else**. "about 5 minutes" and "5 minutes or so" aren't exact. Your pattern should exclude them, and it should handle the spelling variants you found above.

Then filter to the matches, extract the number into a column called `minutes`, convert it to a column called `text_seconds`, and save the result as `minute_data`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
minute_data <- ufo %>%
  filter(str_detect(duration_clean, minute_pattern)) %>%
  mutate(
    minutes = str_extract(
      duration_clean,
      "(?<=^|\\s)\\d+(\\.\\d+)?(?=\\s*(minutes?|mins?)\\.?$)"
    ),
    minutes = as.numeric(minutes),
    text_seconds = minutes * 60
  )
```

> What does `str_extract()` return: a number or a string?
>
> a string

> What are you relying on when you convert minutes to seconds?
>
> that one minute and 60 seconds are the same

## Check it against `encounter_length`

`encounter_length` is supposed to be the same quantity, in seconds. Compare it to your `text_seconds`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

minute_data %>% 
  summarise(
    agree = sum(abs(encounter_length - text_seconds) < 0.0001, na.rm = TRUE),
    disagree = sum(
      abs(encounter_length - text_seconds) >= 0.0001,
    ),
    cannot_compare = sum(is.na(encounter_length))
  )

```

> How many rows of `minute_data` agree? How many disagree? How many can't be compared?
>
> all agree but one (8.2 minutes), just the one cannot be compared because of it being an outlier point (8.2\*60=492 sec)

> If one person typed "5 minutes" and someone else separately recorded 300 seconds, would they agree every single time across tens of thousands of reports?
>
> no, because as humans we fault in errors for different ways of saying and puttinfg things down

> Did you just validate your rule, or rediscover someone else's? What does that tell you about where `encounter_length` came from?
>
> i think i just rediscovered the rule that way used to make uop encounter_length, it probably came from a text recorded time instead of a measurement of time

## Seconds, too

Adapt your pattern to find exact numbers of **seconds**. Extract the number and keep it in seconds. (Do hours too if you want to go further.)

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
second_pattern <- "^\\s*(\\d+(\\.\\d+)?)\\s*(seconds?|secs?)\\.?\\s*$"

second_data <- ufo %>%
  filter(str_detect(duration_clean, second_pattern)) %>%
  mutate(
    seconds = str_extract(
      duration_clean,
      "(?<=^|\\s)\\d+(\\.\\d+)?(?=\\s*(seconds?|secs?)\\.?$)"
    ),
    text_seconds = as.numeric(seconds)
  )
```

> What did your patterns miss? Find descriptions that clearly contain a duration but that neither pattern caught.
>
> missed patterns include ones like when the number was spelled out, a range of time, or phrases

## The ones you can't resolve

Find the descriptions that contain a range with values separated by a hyphen. Count them and look at the most common.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false 

range_ufo <- ufo %>%
  filter(str_detect(duration_clean, "\\d+\\s*-\\s*\\d+")) %>%
  select(described_encounter_length, duration_clean, encounter_length)

nrow(range_ufo)
```

Consider "2-3 minutes." You could call it 120 seconds, 150, or 180.

> What assumption would each choice require? Is any of them defensible from the text alone?
>
> its a minimum, midpoint, or maximum decision but I don't think that's defensible from the text because we have no idea where in the range the time measurement actually falls

Now compare those range descriptions to `encounter_length`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

range_ufo_data <- ufo %>%
  filter(str_detect(duration_clean, "\\d+\\s*-\\s*\\d+")) %>%
  mutate(
    high = as.numeric(str_extract(duration_clean, "(?<=-)\\d+"))
  )
range_ufo_data %>% 
  mutate(
    high_seconds = if_else(
      str_detect(duration_clean, "min"),
      high * 60,
      high
    )
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    agree = sum(encounter_length == high_seconds, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

9613/ nrow(ufo)
```

> Is there a consistent rule connecting the text to the number? What is it? Where is it documented?
>
> it seems to be on a higher end of the range, its found in the data at the longer times

> What proportion of all reports contain a range?
>
> about 12%

> If you computed a median sighting length from `encounter_length`, in which direction would it be wrong, and why?

# Bringing it together

A friend hears you've been working with UFO data and asks: *when do people see UFOs, and how long does a sighting usually last?*

Write a short answer, roughly 200 words, that:

- answers both questions
- says what this data is actually measuring
- tells them the one or two things they'd need to know before trusting your numbers

Based off all the work above from this data set the most common time people see UFOs are in the evening, specifically from the time range 8-11 PM. The busiest time would be 9PM, with 11,445 reports. Saturday is the most common day of the week with reports. July is the most common month with reports. The specific day where the most sightings occur are on July 4th, which is probably influenced by the activities of the holiday (fireworks, outside, and drinking). The patterns suggest the data set is measures of people reporting things they think were UFOs, instead of measuring how often objects appeared in the sky. For duration, the central value of the encounter_length value was 180 seconds (3 minutes). The duration/times are text reported rather than actual number measurements. Within the time there were a lot of ranges (ex: 2-3 minutes), this appeared the most towards the longer sighting times. This could make the time look longer than it actually is. Throughout this reasearch I have had to remind myself that the data is self-reported observations, so knowing this is not the same thing as UFO activity. Also be aware of the ranges and small descriptions when looking at the values given.
